name: Livraria Lello
label: Livraria Lello
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/12514092225: the OpenStreetMap point 'Lello & Irmao Bookstore'.
notes: Neo-Gothic bookshop with a famous red staircase.

text.description: Livraria Lello is a bookshop that opened in 1906 on Rua das Carmelitas, and it is one of the oldest bookshops in Portugal. It is often ranked among the best in the world. It photographs well because the building is full of detail, outside and in. The facade mixes Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau touches. Painted figures representing Art and Science sit above the entrance arch, with the firm's name in bright lettering and small pinnacles along the top. Inside, a forked staircase curves up to a wooden-balustraded gallery. Above it is a large stained glass window measuring 8 by 3.5 metres, carrying the motto Decus in Labore. The ceilings and walls are painted plaster made to look like carved wood, and the small rails and wooden cart once used to move books between the shelves are still there. For your phone, there are two kinds of picture here. Outside, you want the whole front, and then close crops of the painted figures and pinnacles. Inside, you want the staircase, the stained glass and the curved lines of the gallery. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. Entry to the shop has been charged since 2015, so check the official site before you go, including what is allowed for photos inside. It can get busy, so be patient when waiting for a clear view of the staircase.
text.geographic_location: Livraria Lello is in central Porto, on Rua das Carmelitas, facing the Praça de Lisboa. It is a short stroll from the Clérigos Church and tower and close to the University of Porto's Faculty of Sciences building.
text.directions_text: Head for the Clérigos Church and tower, which are near the bookshop, then walk to the Praça de Lisboa, where the bookshop faces onto Rua das Carmelitas. The phone icon on the map is at the bookshop itself, so once you reach the front door you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in from where you stand, and for the staircase inside. Use the default lens (1x) for general views and details such as the balusters. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the painted figures and pinnacles above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the facade from here, stepping back only as far as you need to fit the whole front in the shot. For the interior, stand near the foot of the forked staircase, if the queue and the rules on the day allow it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade's edges up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. For the staircase, hold the phone upright, centre the curve of the steps and include some of the stained glass at the top. Then take a closer shot of the painted figures above the entrance arch, using the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stained glass window to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the glass does not wash out. If the interior is dim, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer, with fewer people in your frame. The facade faces south, so it is likely to be in direct sun around midday.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed bookshop, and entry has been charged since 2015, so check the official site before you go for current entry and photo rules.

name: Porto Cathedral
label: Porto Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terreiro da Sé' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Terreiro da Sé' (way/210470759): middle (148 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/210461448: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Porto Cathedral' (77 m across).
notes: Hilltop Romanesque cathedral with cloisters and city views.

text.description:
Porto Cathedral is a Roman Catholic church in the old centre of the city. It is one of Porto's oldest buildings and one of its most important Romanesque ones. It was built on the site of an old chapel or hermitage founded in 1108. The present church was begun in the second half of the 12th century, and work carried on until the 16th. The 18th century then brought major Baroque changes, including a new main portal in 1772 and a loggia by Nicolau Nasoni on the side façade in 1736. King John I married Philippa of Lancaster here in 1387.

It photographs well because of its shape. Two square towers topped with cupolas flank a plain, heavy front with a Romanesque rose window under a crenellated arch, so the whole building looks a little like a fortress. That makes the classic postcard view.

Keep the phone level and let the towers fill the upper part of the picture, with the cross low in the frame. The square gets busy, so go early if you want it clear of people. If you have time, the sloping street Calçada Dom Pedro Pitões gives a closer, steeper view of the towers above the rooftops.
text.geographic_location: Porto Cathedral stands in the historic centre of Porto, on the square called Terreiro da Sé, which is in front of its main façade.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the historic centre of Porto and ask for Terreiro da Sé, the square in front of the cathedral. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the full twin-towered façade and the stone cross in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and tower tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Terreiro da Sé (right-hand corner of the square, facing the cathedral front). The cathedral's twin-towered façade in the background, with a stone cross in the middle of the square in the foreground. In the right-hand corner of the square, facing the cathedral front. From here you see the twin-towered façade in the background, with the stone cross in the middle of the square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the phone upright so the towers stay straight. Put the cross low in the frame as a lead-in, with the façade filling the upper two thirds. For a second picture, try the sloping street Calçada Dom Pedro Pitões, which gives a closer view of the towers above the old-town roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus and drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the square fills up with other visitors.

text.access_note: The square is open at all hours and free, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements inside.

text.description:
Bolhão Market is a market in Porto and is ranked 3 on the Porto shot map. It is a good place for lively, colourful phone photos. Depending on the day, you might find stacked fruit and vegetables, flower stalls, fish counters, hand-written signs and stallholders at work. The phone icon on the map sits at the market itself, so you can start shooting as soon as you arrive.

Work in layers. Take one wide shot to show the setting and the crowd. Then step closer for a single stall, a pile of produce or a price sign. Markets are busy places, so keep moving gently, stay out of the way of people shopping and carrying goods, and ask politely before pointing your phone at a stallholder's face. Many people are happy to be photographed if you smile and ask first.

Light in a market can vary between bright and shaded areas. Tap on the part of the scene you care about most and nudge the exposure slider until the food looks natural rather than washed out. If you want a quiet frame without people, arriving early or at a slower moment of the day usually helps. Rules about photography, opening days and which areas are open to visitors can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Café Majestic is a historic café on Rua de Santa Catarina, in Porto. It opened in 1922 and was designed by the architect José Pinto de Oliveira to look like a Parisian café, in the Art Nouveau style. At first it was an exclusive, upmarket place where the city's elite met. After decades of decline it was recognised as a building of national historical interest in 1983. Major restoration followed, and it reopened in July 1994 in its original Belle Époque style.

It photographs well because the building is full of decorative detail, which gives you plenty to work with. You can take a wide shot of the whole frontage, then move in on the ornate details around the entrance and windows. If you go inside, a few close shots of the decor and table settings tell the story of the place well.

If the street is busy, be patient and wait for a gap in the passers-by. Keep your phone straight and use the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building do not lean. Whether photos are welcome inside, or at busy times, is up to the café, so check with the café before you go and be polite to other guests.

name: Clérigos Church
label: Clérigos Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rua dos Clérigos' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rua dos Clérigos nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223780953: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Igreja dos Clérigos' (45 m across).
notes: Baroque church with Porto's tallest landmark tower.

text.description:
The Clérigos Church is a Baroque church in the middle of Porto, and its tall bell tower is one of the city's best-known landmarks. Nicolau Nasoni, an Italian architect and painter, designed it for the Brotherhood of the Clérigos. Building ran from 1732 to 1750, and the tower and the double stairway in front were finished in 1763. The tower stands about 75 metres tall, and you can see it from many parts of the city.

It photographs well because the main facade is richly decorated with garlands, shells and a broken pediment, and the tower rises behind it. The side walls also show the church's almost oval floor plan. Stand a little way down the street and face up toward the church, so the facade and tower rise at the end of the street with the building a short distance ahead. It is about 42 metres from the church. Backing away gives you the whole tower in one frame, which is hard to manage close up.

The street can be busy, so give yourself a minute to wait for a clear gap. If you want a more distant view, Praça da Liberdade shows the church and tower from further away, and works best with your phone's zoom. If you climb the tower, you can look down on the oval nave from the high gallery, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The tower rises behind the church and can be seen from many parts of the city.
text.directions_text: From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the church steps. Walk up the street facing west and you will see the facade and tower ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and tower together. Switch to 2x or 3x, if your phone has it, for a tighter picture of the tower from the same spot. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you are close to the building or on the stairway, and expect the tower to lean in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua dos Clérigos (stand further down the street, facing up toward the church). The Baroque facade and tower rising at the end of the street, with the church in the distance. From here the Baroque facade and tower rise at the end of the street. The church is a short walk ahead, so do not go right up to it for this shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Hold the phone level and do not tilt it up too much, or the tower will lean back. Use the street's buildings on both sides as a frame. For a different view, try Praça da Liberdade with the zoom, which gives a distant shot of the church and tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots, because people walking through the frame will change from one to the next.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the day if you can, as the street is likely to be busier around late morning and early afternoon.

text.access_note: The church is open to the public to visit and the street is open public space, but the tower climb is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

label: Ribeira
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cais da Ribeira' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Cais da Ribeira nearest the subject (our map tiles).

text.description: Ribeira Square (Praça da Ribeira) is the old riverside square of Porto's Ribeira district, within the historic centre that UNESCO lists as World Heritage. It photographs well because the arcaded house fronts, the Douro and the Dom Luís I Bridge all sit close together, so one frame can hold a lot of Porto. The buildings around the square were rebuilt with arcades after a fire in 1491. The square was reorganised between 1776 and 1782, and the medieval walls on the river side were pulled down in 1821, which opened it to the water. In the northern part of the square you can find a three-storey fountain from the 1780s with a statue of St John the Baptist. The square also has a modern cube-shaped sculpture nicknamed the Cubo da Ribeira. From there you get a wider view of the waterfront and its facades with the bridge behind, and usually fewer people in the frame. The square is popular with visitors, so go early if you want clear shots. If you want a higher view looking down on the rooftops and river, Miradouro da Vitória is a good alternative.
text.geographic_location: In the Ribeira district of Porto's historic centre, on the Douro waterfront in the São Nicolau parish. The Dom Luís I Bridge rises behind the riverside promenade.
text.directions_text: There is no Metro or tram stop at this spot, so head for the Ribeira waterfront in Porto's historic centre. Walk to the eastern end of the riverside promenade, Cais da Ribeira, and stop where the crowd thins out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the waterfront, the facades and the bridge into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the house fronts. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the fountain or the Cubo da Ribeira.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cais da Ribeira (eastern end of the riverside promenade, past the main tourist cluster). A wider angle of the Ribeira waterfront and facades with the Dom Luís I Bridge behind, and fewer people in the frame than at the central stretch. At the eastern end of the riverside promenade, past the main tourist cluster. From there the square lies just to the north, and you look along the Ribeira facades with the Dom Luís I Bridge behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the rows of facades up with them so the buildings stand straight. Keep the bridge in the upper part of the frame and the water or promenade in the lower part. Wait for a gap in the crowd before you press the shutter. If you want a high view over the rooftops and river instead, Miradouro da Vitória is another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facades to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Use night mode only if the light fades and your hands are steady. Hold the phone against your body or a railing for sharper results.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the Ribeira facades are lit directly and the riverside is quieter.

name: Dom Luís I Bridge
label: Dom Luís I Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar' (relation/4673533): middle (105 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/835566871: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte Luiz I' (417 m across).
notes: Iconic double-deck iron arch bridge over the Douro.

text.description:
Dom Luís I Bridge is the shape that defines Porto's riverside: a double-deck iron arch crossing the Douro between Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia. When it was built, its 172-metre arch span was the longest of its type in the world. The upper deck opened in 1886 and the lower deck followed a year later. It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, who also designed the nearby Maria Pia Bridge, so the two look alike. Today the upper deck carries pedestrians and Porto Metro line D, while the lower deck is for buses, taxis, cyclists and pedestrians.

The best full view is from the terrace in front of the Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar on the Gaia side. From here you see the whole profile of the arch, with the Porto skyline and the old hillside spread out behind it. Several guides call it the best panoramic view of the bridge in the city. The climb up is steep, so allow some time and a rest at the top.

For your photo, keep the whole arch in one frame and let the city fill the background. If you want something different, Jardim do Morro shows the bridge against the Porto hillside, and Miradouro da Vitória shows it beside the cathedral and the Ribeira rooftops. Jardim do Morro gets very crowded at sunset.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Douro between Porto's Ribeira and cathedral area and the Vila Nova de Gaia waterfront. The Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar stands on the Gaia hill beside the bridge's upper deck.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk to the Serra do Pilar monastery from Porto city centre or the Gaia waterfront. The monastery sits beside the southern end of the bridge's upper deck, so you can also walk across the upper deck from the Porto side. The final climb to the terrace is steep. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which should fit most of the arch and the skyline behind it. If you are close to the terrace wall and the bridge gets cut off at the sides, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out the bridge against the hillside.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar (Terrace in front of the monastery, Vila Nova de Gaia side). The full profile of the bridge's double-deck arch with the Porto skyline and historic hillside spread behind it. On the Vila Nova de Gaia side, and look across towards the bridge. From here the whole double-deck arch is in view, with the Porto skyline and the historic hillside behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch along the lower third of the frame, so the city rises behind it. Keep the horizon level, because the long deck lines show any tilt. For a different angle, try Jardim do Morro, which shows the bridge with the Porto hillside behind it, or Miradouro da Vitória, which frames the bridge against the cathedral and the Ribeira rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. For a night shot, use night mode and rest your phone on the terrace wall to keep it steady. A Metro tram crossing the upper deck can make a nice moving detail, so take a few shots as it passes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day. Some guides recommend golden hour from the Gaia side, others sunrise from the Ribeira side. If you want a night shot, check first that the bridge lights are on, as one visitor found them switched off at midnight in summer.

text.access_note: The bridge decks are open to pedestrians and the terrace is outdoors, but check the official site before you go for the monastery grounds and for any works on the bridge.

label: Palácio da Bolsa

notes: Neoclassical stock exchange with the ornate Arab Room.

text.description:
The Palácio da Bolsa, or Stock Exchange Palace, is a grand Neoclassical building in the historic centre of Porto, on Infante D. Henrique Square. It was built in the 19th century by the city's Commercial Association, and its calm, symmetrical front is easy to photograph. The palace stands beside the St Francis Church. The site was once a convent, and a fire in 1832 destroyed its cloisters. In 1841 Queen Mary II gave the ruins to the city's merchants, building began in 1842, and most of the palace was finished by 1850. The interior decoration was only completed in 1910, and the palace has been a National Monument since 1982.

For photos, the outside gives you a stately facade with strong lines, which suits a phone's gridlines well. Step back across the square to fit more of the building in, then move closer for details of the stonework and doorway. If you visit the interior, the highlights are the Nations' Courtyard, covered by a large octagonal metal and glass dome, and the Arab Room, decorated in Moorish Revival style. Both are very photogenic, but indoor access and photo rules can change, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone steady against a wall or rail in dim rooms, and remember that a tour group may be moving through the space.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Porto, on Infante D. Henrique Square, right beside the St Francis Church.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the historic centre of Porto and head for Infante D. Henrique Square, where the palace stands next to the St Francis Church. The phone icon on the map is at the palace itself, so once you are at the building you have arrived. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want to include the square. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you are right at the building, so take close-up shots of the entrance and stonework. For the whole facade, walk back across the square and shoot towards the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the facade's vertical edges with them, keeping the phone level so the building does not lean. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) from close range, but keep the building centred to limit distortion. If you go inside, try pointing the ultra-wide lens up at the Nations' Courtyard dome, and the default lens (1x) for the Arab Room.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Indoors, use night mode only if you can hold the phone very still, and check first whether photography is allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outdoors, pick a time when the facade is evenly lit and the square is quieter, such as earlier in the day. Indoors, visiting times depend on the official schedule.

text.access_note: The palace is a historic building where interior access is likely to be controlled, so check the official site before you go; the square outside is open public space.

name: Church of São Francisco
label: São Francisco Church
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/210681249: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of São Francisco' (60 m across).
notes: Gothic church with a dazzling gilded Baroque interior.

text.description:
The Church of São Francisco (Igreja de São Francisco) is the most prominent Gothic monument in Porto. It is also known for the Baroque decoration inside. It stands in the city's historic centre, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Franciscans came to Porto around 1223. The present church was begun in 1383 under King Ferdinand I and finished around 1425. Because the structure has barely changed since, it is the best example of Gothic architecture in the city.

For photos, the outside is the part to aim for. The main façade has a large, elaborate Gothic rose window, the only original decoration on that front. Below it is a Baroque west portal with twisted (solomonic) columns and a statue of St Francis. The south portal, facing the river, is still Gothic, with a stepped-forward opening and a triangular gable. Next door are the 18th-century Church of the Ordem Terceira de São Francisco and the Order's Dispatch House, which gives you neighbouring buildings to include for context.

Inside, almost every surface is covered in gilded woodwork (talha dourada) from the first half of the 18th century. It hides much of the medieval architecture and is considered among the finest in Portugal. Rules on photography inside, and whether entry is ticketed, can change, so check the official site before you go. Outside, take a few shots at different distances: one wide for the whole façade, one closer for the rose window and portal.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Porto, beside the Palácio da Bolsa (the Stock Exchange Palace), which stands where the church's old cloisters once were.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or train stop right at this spot, so head for the historic centre of Porto and look for the Palácio da Bolsa, which stands right next to the church. Once there, the church is easy to recognise by its Gothic rose window. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade in when you are close. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the front and portal. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and carved portal details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Outside, step back from the façade until the rose window and portal both fit comfortably in the frame. To photograph the Gothic south portal, go round to the river side of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central door and rose window up with the middle vertical line, keeping your phone level so the walls do not lean. Try one wide shot with the neighbouring buildings and one tighter shot of the rose window. Inside, if photography is allowed, use the telephoto to pick out single carved altarpieces such as the Tree of Jesse rather than trying to capture the whole gilded nave.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Inside, where it is dim, hold the phone steady against a pillar or your body. Night mode, if it switches on, will brighten the gold, but keep still while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the stone façade. Mornings or an overcast day tend to avoid harsh shadows on the rose window.

text.access_note: The church may be ticketed and may have rules on photography and dress inside, so check the official site before you go.

name: Casa da Música
label: Casa da Música
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida da Boavista' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenida da Boavista nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/603359226: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa da Música' (104 m across).
notes: Angular concert hall designed by Rem Koolhaas.

text.description:
Casa da Música is Porto's concert hall, designed by the architect Rem Koolhaas and opened in 2005. It looks like a huge, faceted white block that has landed in the middle of the Boavista district. It is a nine-floor asymmetrical shape clad in white cement, cut by large glass windows. It was built on the site of the old tram terminus at the Rotunda da Boavista, and it sits well back from the street on a wide open plaza of marble.

It photographs well because the angles change as you move, and the plain white surfaces show every shadow. The building is also about 104 m across, so it only fits in a frame if you step back. For the full faceted front, walk back toward Avenida da Boavista. Guides recommend the avenue, opposite the facade, for the widest view.

For a second view, try the Jardim da Rotunda da Boavista. The hall sits against the greenery there, and the nearby monument adds a contrast in shape and age. The rooftop terrace gives a view down over the roundabout and its column, with the tiled terrace floor in the foreground. You reach it through the building and access depends on opening hours and house rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Casa da Música stands in the Boavista district of Porto, at the Rotunda da Boavista. It is set back from Avenida da Boavista, on the site of the old tram terminus.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Rotunda da Boavista, the big roundabout in the Boavista district. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you want straighter, more natural edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the angled white faces and the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida da Boavista (standing across the avenue from the building, opposite the facade). The full faceted white-concrete facade, framed against the city backdrop. For a wider view, step back toward Avenida da Boavista.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up so its base sits along a horizontal line. Keep your phone upright and level, so the vertical edges don't lean. Leave a little sky above the roof and some plaza below for scale. For a different version, walk to the Jardim da Rotunda da Boavista and frame the hall behind the greenery and the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the concrete stays bright white without losing the shadows between the facets. Take a few shots as you move, since the angles change from step to step.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is lower in the sky. Raking light picks out the facets of the white concrete. A clear sky also helps the white stand out against the city.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public street and plaza. The rooftop terrace is reached through the building and depends on opening hours and house rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Low, angled sunlight tends to bring out the facets of white concrete.
Photographing the exterior is encouraged, but flash and recording during performances are banned.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can stretch or tilt vertical lines near the edges of the frame, so keeping the phone level helps.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright white surfaces from washing out.
Guides recommend Avenida da Boavista, opposite the facade, as the best place for a full-facade view.

name: São Bento railway station
label: São Bento Station
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5391639447: the OpenStreetMap point 'Porto - São Bento'.
notes: Station hall covered in blue azulejo tiles.

text.description:
São Bento is a working railway terminal in the middle of Porto's Historic Centre, and the main reason to photograph it is the entrance hall. The walls are covered in about 20,000 azulejo tiles, painted by Jorge Colaço and fired in the Sacavém factory. They were put up between 1905 and 1916 and cover roughly 551 square metres. Most of the big scenes are in blue on white and show moments from Portuguese history, including the Battle of Valdevez and King John I arriving in Porto for his wedding in 1387. Above them runs a coloured band showing how people travelled in different parts of the country, and the entrance wall has small countryside panels.

The building itself is granite, in the French-influenced Beaux-Arts style, designed by the Porto architect José Marques da Silva. Work began in 1904, and the whole project, structure and decoration, took 13 years. It stands where a Benedictine convent once stood, which is where the name São Bento (Saint Benedict) comes from.

For a phone photo, the tile walls give you strong blue and white shapes and plenty of small detail. Try one wide shot to show the scale of the hall, then move closer for single panels. Keep to the sides of the hall so you don't block people catching trains, and turn on the gridlines so the tall edges of the panels stay straight.
text.geographic_location: São Bento is in the Historic Centre of Porto, on Praça Almeida Garrett, next to Rua da Madeira and Rua do Loureiro. The hill of Batalha rises directly behind it.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is at the station itself, so there is no walk once you arrive. The Porto Metro's São Bento station on line D is linked to the railway station by an underground link. Otherwise, walk to Praça Almeida Garrett and go in through the main entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a whole wall of tiles into one picture. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a single large panel. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces, horses and the small countryside panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your wide shots from the middle of the entrance hall, then walk to either side for the panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the panels so the walls look straight. Hold the phone level and at chest height, because tilting it upwards will make the walls lean inwards. Keep the blue scenes in the middle of the frame and let the coloured band of transport scenes sit across the top. For the outside, step back into the square so the whole granite front fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a tile panel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright windows or doorway wash out the blue and white. If the hall is dim, use night mode and hold still for the few seconds it needs. Avoid panorama inside, as it can bend the straight lines of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quieter moment such as early morning or later in the day, when fewer people are in the hall. The hall is lit from inside and the light is fairly even, so you can photograph it at any time of day.

text.access_note: This is a working railway station, so check the official site before you go for any access rules and for when the entrance hall is open to visitors.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or later in the day is usually quieter in the entrance hall than midday.
The entrance hall is lit from inside and gives fairly even light at most times of day.
Visitors can usually walk into the entrance hall of the station, but this should be checked on the official site.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards, and panorama mode can bend straight lines.

photo.artist: Jose Goncalves / Joseolgon at Portuguese Wikipedia

name: Funicular dos Guindais
label: Guindais Funicular
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Muralha Fernandina' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1372762674: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Funicular dos Guindais' (295 m across).
notes: Short funicular linking Ribeira with the upper town.

text.description:
The Funicular dos Guindais is a short railway that links Praça da Batalha in the upper city with the Cais dos Guindais by the River Douro. The current line opened on 19 February 2004, following the path of an earlier funicular that ran briefly in the 19th century. It runs alongside the remains of the Fernandine Walls, so you get old stone, a steep green slope and a modern cabin in one frame. Two cars, each carrying up to 25 people, pass one another on the single track, and the ride takes about two and a half minutes. The photo works because the Dom Luís I Bridge sits behind the slope and gives the picture a clear sense of place.

For a photo that doesn't need a ticket, use the outside garden of the Muralha Fernandina, near the upper station. From the garden the funicular climbs the slope in front of you with the bridge as the backdrop, and you can walk there easily once you leave the upper station. Cars run about every 10 minutes, so choose your frame first and wait for one to appear. Keep the bridge's lines level using the gridlines. A photo from inside the cabin is also possible, but it needs a paid ride. Confirm that the funicular is running before you go, as it has been closed for maintenance at times.
text.geographic_location: In the Batalha and Ribeira area of Porto, on the slope between Praça da Batalha above and the riverside below, beside the remains of the Fernandine Walls and close to the lower level of the Dom Luís I Bridge.
text.directions_text: Head for Praça da Batalha, where the upper funicular station stands by the end of the vintage tram line 22, and São Bento station is within walking distance. The garden of the Muralha Fernandina lies just outside the upper station, with the slope falling away towards the river. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the funicular on its slope with the bridge behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the wall and garden in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single car against the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the view described here, stand in the outside garden of the Muralha Fernandina, near the upper funicular station. From the garden the funicular runs up the slope in front of you with the Dom Luís I Bridge behind it. The name may appear on the map as Muralhas Fernandinas.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the track along one third of the frame, so the bridge sits level behind it. Wait for a car to enter the shot, which happens about every 10 minutes. Include a bit of the old wall or garden in the foreground for depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the car or the slope to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and bridge keep their detail. Try a Live Photo so you can pick the best moment as the car passes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, and fewer people in the garden. Check that the funicular is running first.

text.access_note: The garden outside the upper station is a public outdoor space, but the funicular ride is ticketed and its running times can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep sky and bridge detail.
Live Photos let you choose the best frame as a car passes.

name: Liberdade Square
label: Praça da Liberdade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida dos Aliados' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenida dos Aliados nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14169426: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Praça da Liberdade' (78 m across).
notes: Square with the equestrian statue of Pedro IV.

text.description:
Liberdade Square (Praça da Liberdade) is one of the main squares in Porto's lower town, the Baixa. It runs straight into Avenida dos Aliados at its north side. The square began as Praça Nova, a new square planned in the early 1700s. Its oldest surviving building is the grand Neoclassical front of the former Lóios convent, now the Cardosas Palace, which closes the south side. In the middle stands a bronze statue of King Pedro IV on horseback, put up in 1866. It is by the French sculptor Anatole Calmels, and the king holds the Constitution he fought to protect.

For a phone photo, the best-known picture here is the large blue 'PORTO' sign with the Town Hall behind it, framed by the Aliados buildings. It makes an easy souvenir shot, and the tall façades give you a strong frame for people in the foreground. Turn to the south-west and the square, with the statue and the old buildings, makes a second picture from the same spot. Guides do not agree on exactly where the sign stands, so check the spot on the map. Building work around the square may block some angles. The square is lined with banks, hotels, restaurants and offices, so expect people walking through your frame. Wait a moment for a gap rather than rushing the shot.
text.geographic_location: Liberdade Square is in the Baixa, Porto's lower town, in the Santo Ildefonso parish. It sits at the southern end of Avenida dos Aliados and is not far from São Bento Train Station.
text.directions_text: Head for the Baixa, the lower town, and look for the south end of Avenida dos Aliados, where it meets Liberdade Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the 'PORTO' sign with the Town Hall behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole square, or use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida dos Aliados (near the large blue 'PORTO' sign in front of the Town Hall (Câmara Municipal)). The large blue 'PORTO' letters with the city's Town Hall behind them, framed by the Aliados buildings and the top end of the square. The exact position of the sign is uncertain, so check the map. From here the photo shows the blue letters with the Town Hall behind them, framed by the Aliados buildings and the top end of the square. The middle of the square, with the statue, is to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the letters in the lower part of the picture and let the Town Hall rise behind them. Turn to the south-west for a second shot of the Pedro IV statue with the grand façades behind. For a long view up the avenue instead, stand on Avenida dos Aliados and look towards the square, with the Cardosas building at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines so the tall buildings stand straight. Tap the sign to focus, then use the exposure slider if the sky washes out the Town Hall. For the statue, tap on the bronze and keep your phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you want fewer people in front of the sign. Check the map for work around the square first.

text.access_note: This is an open public square and avenue, so no ticket is needed. Reviews mention building work around the square, so check the map for blocked angles.
claims_not_in_sources: Going early in the day is likely to mean fewer people in front of the 'PORTO' sign.
The square and avenue are open to the public with no ticket needed.
Turning to the south-west from the stand-here point gives a view across the square towards the statue.

name: Gaia Cable Car
label: Gaia Cable Car
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardim do Morro' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardim do Morro' (node/335557216): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107436948: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Teleférico de Gaia' (534 m long).
notes: Cable car above the Gaia riverfront with views over the Douro.

text.description:
The Gaia Cable Car (Teleférico de Gaia) is a gondola lift on the Vila Nova de Gaia bank of the Douro, facing Porto across the water. Its little cabins run between the riverside promenade at Cais de Gaia and the high ground by Jardim do Morro. The line is about 562 metres long, rises to roughly 63 metres above sea level at the top, and opened in April 2011. There are 12 cars, and the ride takes under four minutes. The cars normally travel slowly, so the view stays in place long enough to take a few frames of one cabin.

It photographs well because the car, the river and Porto's skyline can all sit in one picture. The best place for this is the terrace beside the upper station, where you can watch a cabin arrive or leave with the Dom Luís I Bridge and the Porto rooftops behind it. A longer lens helps here, so use your phone's telephoto (2x to 5x if it has it) and wait for a car to drift into the gap you have framed. If you want something different, Cais de Gaia on the waterfront looks up towards the lower station, with Ribeira and the bridge across the river. Miradouro do Teleférico is another option, showing the upper station and a cabin arriving with the old-town rooftops behind. Early morning or the golden hour before sunset gives the nicest light.
text.geographic_location: In Vila Nova de Gaia, on the south bank of the Douro opposite Porto. The upper station sits beside Jardim do Morro, the upper level of the Dom Luís I Bridge and the Serra do Pilar Monastery, and the lower station is on the Cais de Gaia promenade.
text.directions_text: Head for Jardim do Morro in Vila Nova de Gaia, on the south side of the river from Porto. By taxi or hired scooter, ask to be dropped at Jardim do Morro, where the upper station is next to Jardim do Morro Metro station. From there, the middle of the cable line is to the west, and walking down towards the waterfront and the lower station takes you along the line. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pull the cabin, the river and the Porto skyline into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider view of the station terrace, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardim do Morro (terrace beside the upper cable car station, Vila Nova de Gaia side). The gondola arriving or leaving the upper station, shot with a telephoto lens so the car, the Douro and the Porto skyline and bridge sit in one frame. On the terrace beside the upper cable car station.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the cable line on one of them so the cabin has space to move into. Wait for a car to approach the station, with the bridge and the Ribeira rooftops behind it, then take several shots. For a different view, try Cais de Gaia on the waterfront, looking up at the lower station and the car climbing away from the quay, or Miradouro do Teleférico, which shows the upper station with the old town behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cabin to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the car does not look washed out. Try a Live Photo or a burst when a car moves across the frame, then choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the golden hour before sunset.

text.access_note: Jardim do Morro is a free public garden, but the cable car itself is a ticketed ride, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Porto skyline and the Dom Luís I Bridge lie across the river from the upper-station terrace and can appear behind the cabin from there.
A telephoto lens on a phone (2x to 5x) compresses the view so that the cabin, river and skyline appear together in one frame.
Early morning and the golden hour before sunset give the best light for photographing the cable car.

name: Maria Pia Bridge
label: Maria Pia Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar' (relation/4673533): middle (105 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/835569085: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte de Dona Maria Pia' (370 m across).
notes: Historic railway arch bridge designed by Eiffel's firm.

text.description:
Maria Pia Bridge is a slender wrought-iron arch that carries nothing now but still draws the eye across the Douro. It was built in the 1870s and is attributed to Gustave Eiffel. King Luís I and Queen Maria Pia opened it in November 1878, and it was named after her. When it was finished it was the longest single-arch span in the world. The arch rises about 60 m above the river, and the bridge ran as a railway line until 1991, when the nearby São João Bridge took over. People often mistake it for the Dom Luís I bridge. That one was built nine years later, lies about a kilometre downstream and has two decks.

You can't walk on Maria Pia, so every photo of it is a view from a distance. The best-known view is from the circular terrace in front of the Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar, on the Vila Nova de Gaia side. From there the Dom Luís I bridge fills the foreground in profile, the Maria Pia arch sits further upriver, and the Porto skyline rises around it. Guides call it the best panoramic bridge view in the city, and it gives the wide, postcard-style shot. The Maria Pia arch is small in the frame, so decide whether you want the whole panorama or a closer crop of the arch. Alternatives are the Dom Luís I deck, where you must stay clear of the tram tracks, and the Miradouro das Fontaínhas, which shows several bridges at once.
text.geographic_location: The bridge itself spans the river between Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia, upriver from the Dom Luís I bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar in Vila Nova de Gaia. Once on the terrace, look east along the river and the Maria Pia arch is beyond the Dom Luís I bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full scene of both bridges and the skyline, then use telephoto (3x-5x if your phone has it) to pull the Maria Pia arch closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the terrace and the monastery behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar (circular terrace in front of the monastery, Vila Nova de Gaia side, looking east along the river). The Dom Luís I bridge in profile in the foreground, with the Maria Pia arch further upriver to the east and the Porto skyline around it. The Dom Luís I bridge is in the foreground, with the Maria Pia arch further upriver and the Porto skyline around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Dom Luís I bridge along the lower third, with the Maria Pia arch higher up and toward the far side so the two bridges read as separate shapes. Keep the horizon level. For a tighter picture, zoom in on the arch with the river below it. If you have time, the Dom Luís I deck or the Miradouro das Fontaínhas gives a different angle on the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the iron stays dark. Hold the phone steady against a wall or railing when zoomed in, as a distant arch blurs easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Several guides suggest sunset for this view. Looking east, the evening light should fall on the bridge from behind you. Check the light on the day, as haze can flatten the view.

text.access_note: The terrace in front of the monastery is an open public space; check the official site before you go if you want to visit the monastery itself, and remember the bridge is closed to walkers.

name: Monastery of Serra do Pilar
label: Serra do Pilar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo de Aviz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Largo de Aviz' (way/98835820): middle (105 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4673533: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar' (106 m across).
notes: Round-cloister monastery with the best panorama of Porto.

text.description:
The Monastery of Serra do Pilar sits on a rocky hill in Vila Nova de Gaia, looking across the Douro to Porto's old town. Its round church is the part you will photograph. It stands 36 m tall and dominates the skyline on the south bank. The cloister is also circular, with the same diameter as the church, which is unusual. The church was inaugurated in 1672, and the monastery was later fortified and used in the wars of the 19th century. It is part of Porto's UNESCO World Heritage listing, and the church still holds Sunday Mass.

It photographs well because of the setting. The Douro, the Dom Luís I Bridge and Porto's riverfront are in the wider view. The long open sides of the square help keep other visitors out of your frame. Keep your phone level so the round walls don't lean, and take a few shots at slightly different distances. If you want a different view, the upper deck of the Ponte Dom Luís I shows the church on its hill above the river. The Rampa do Infante Santo gives a quieter angle of the church at the top of the slope.
text.geographic_location: The monastery is in Vila Nova de Gaia, on the south bank of the Douro directly opposite Porto's historic centre, on the hill above the Dom Luís I Bridge. The open square in front of the church is Largo de Aviz.
text.directions_text: Head for the Vila Nova de Gaia side of the Douro. Jardim do Morro Station on the Porto Metro's D Line gives access to the monastery, and the Gaia Cable Car also runs up from the Gaia riverside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole church and a good amount of sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) when you want a more natural view of the church with the wider scene around it. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the bridge and riverfront in the wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo de Aviz (open area in front of the circular church, facing the Douro). The circular church of the monastery in the foreground, with the Douro, the Dom Luís I Bridge and Porto's riverfront behind it. From here the church sits in the foreground, and the Douro, the Dom Luís I Bridge and Porto's riverfront are in the wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the church up with a vertical grid line so the round walls stay upright. Put the church to one side and let the river, bridge and riverfront show in the wider view. Step back a little before using the ultra-wide, as it exaggerates the tower when you are close. For a different shot, try the upper deck of the Ponte Dom Luís I, or the Rampa do Infante Santo for a quieter view of the church on its hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. If the light is strong behind the church, try a second shot with the default lens (1x) and compare.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is a good time for softer light on the church. Sunsets here get very crowded, so arrive early if you want a clear spot.

text.access_note: The open area in front of the church is a public viewpoint, but the monastery itself includes a church with Sunday Mass and a military area, and the interior may be ticketed or have limited hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer on the white church walls.
Standing close and using the ultra-wide lens exaggerates the tilt of tall buildings.
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) helps pick out the bridge and riverfront in the wider view.
The Rampa do Infante Santo and the bridge deck are alternative viewpoints, with the bridge deck being busier.

name: Sandeman
label: Sandeman Cellars
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo Miguel Bombarda' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Largo de Miguel Bombarda' (way/1079535366): middle (74 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N13684797492 (Sandeman): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous port wine cellar with the caped Don figure in Gaia.

text.description:
This is the Sandeman cellar entrance on the Gaia side of the Douro, and the photo here is the forecourt in front of it. The cellar façade carries the Sandeman sign, and at the entrance stands the caped Don figure. Together they make a clear, recognisable picture of a port cellar, and the open forecourt gives you room to frame it without much clutter around it.

The forecourt is at its best in the morning. Early light and fewer people mean the façade and the statue read cleanly. Tour groups tend to gather here around midday, so if you can, come before then.

Stand on the forecourt, face the entrance and put the Don figure on one side of the frame with the Sandeman sign above or beside him. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building edges stay straight. If you want a different view afterwards, there are two good alternatives. Cais de Gaia, by the river, shows the lodge rooftops with the painted Sandeman name in the foreground, with Ribeira's colourful houses and the Dom Luís I Bridge across the water. Jardim do Morro is higher and wider, looking down onto the same rooftops with the old town and the bridge behind. Note that it is a more distant view of the lodges, not a close-up of the building.

Some cellar terraces on this side may require a purchase, so check what is open to the public before you plan a shot from inside.
text.geographic_location: On the Vila Nova de Gaia bank of the Douro, on Largo Miguel Bombarda, at the entrance to the Sandeman cellar. Ribeira and the Dom Luís I Bridge are across the river.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. It is on Largo Miguel Bombarda on the Gaia side of the Douro. Two addresses are in use for the cellar (Largo Miguel Bombarda 3 and 47), so check which one you are heading for before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the façade and the Don figure together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or the building edges leave you no space, and keep the phone level so the lines don't lean. For a tighter shot of the statue and sign alone, use telephoto (2x) if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo Miguel Bombarda (forecourt in front of the Sandeman cellar entrance, next to the Don statue). The cellar façade with the Sandeman sign and the caped Don figure at the entrance, framed against the forecourt. Look south-east towards the cellar façade with the Sandeman sign and the caped Don figure at the entrance, framed against the forecourt.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Don figure on one third line, with the Sandeman sign filling the upper part of the frame. Keep the building edges straight. For a different shot, try Cais de Gaia for the painted Sandeman name on the lodge rooftops with Ribeira and the bridge behind, or Jardim do Morro for a higher, wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the white sky is washing out the sign. Try portrait mode on the Don figure for a softer background, but check the edges of the cape.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before tour groups gather around midday.

text.access_note: The forecourt in front of the entrance is an open public space, but the cellar and its terraces may require a purchase, so check the official site before you go.

name: Infante Dom Henrique Bridge
label: Infante Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Passeio das Fontainhas' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Passeio das Fontainhas nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/835566537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte Infante Dom Henrique' (412 m across).
notes: Modern concrete arch bridge east of the centre.

text.description: The Infante Dom Henrique Bridge (locally the Ponte do Infante) is a road bridge over the Douro that links Vila Nova de Gaia with central Porto. It was completed in 2003 and sits upriver from the Dom Luís I bridge and downriver from the Maria Pia bridge. It is 371 metres long, with a single arch spanning 280 metres. The deck is 75 metres above the water, but the arch itself rises only about 25 metres from its footings in the cliffs. That makes it one of the flattest arches in the world for its length, and from below it looks like a thin, pale line across the gorge. The bridge photographs well from the riverside promenade on the Porto side, where the arch and deck rise above the water. The Porto riverfront and the Dom Luís I bridge also fit into the frame, and sunset is the time guides recommend. Keep the whole span in view and let the river fill the lower part of the picture. Add a few people or boats on the water for scale. A second option is the quayside along Avenida Gustavo Eiffel, which shows the bridge from river level with the Maria Pia bridge further along. Check the exact stand point on the map before you shoot there.
text.geographic_location: On the Porto side of the Douro, on the riverside promenade below the Infante Dom Henrique Bridge, reached on foot from the Ribeira area.
text.directions_text: Start from the Ribeira area and walk upriver along the Douro to Passeio das Fontainhas. The way can be uphill and uneven in places, so wear comfortable shoes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole arch and the river in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Dom Luís I bridge in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Passeio das Fontainhas (Porto side, on the riverside promenade directly below the bridge). The bridge's arch and deck rising above the river, with the Porto riverfront and the Luís I bridge in the frame, especially at sunset. The bridge's arch and deck rise above the river to the south, with the Porto riverfront and the Luís I bridge in view. If you want an alternative, the quayside along Avenida Gustavo Eiffel shows the bridge from river level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge deck along a horizontal line so it sits level. Keep the arch centred or just off-centre, and leave the water in the lower third. Hold the phone steady against a railing or wall if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sunset colours don't wash out. In dim light after sunset, use night mode and hold still for a couple of seconds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the bridge and the river are at their most atmospheric from this side.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public space, but take care on any upper level of the bridges, where there is no barrier between trains and pedestrians, and take care if you plan to cross.
claims_not_in_sources: The promenade is an open public walkway with no entry fee (the research found no paid viewpoints).
Ultra-wide lenses help fit a long bridge into the frame when you are close to it.
Setting exposure for the sky helps keep sunset colours from washing out.

name: Avenida dos Aliados
label: Avenida dos Aliados
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Praça da Liberdade' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Praça da Liberdade' (relation/14169426): middle (77 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W741944101 (Avenida dos Aliados): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Grand boulevard ending at the City Hall.

text.description: Avenida dos Aliados is the grand avenue in the middle of Porto, lined with imposing buildings, with the City Hall rising behind its façades. It photographs well because of its strong, regular lines, and because the best frames use more than one layer: statues close to you, tall façades behind. For this spot the map sends you to Praça da Liberdade, a short walk south of the avenue. It is a quieter place to take the shot than the avenue itself. If you would like the classic alternative, walk up the avenue itself. There you can frame the 'Porto' sign with the façades and City Hall behind it, or take a symmetrical view straight along the avenue. Check the map before you shoot, because the exact spot of the sign is not pinned down. Building works along the avenue have been mentioned by visitors and may block some angles, so be ready to move a few steps and try another view. Daytime is the best moment, when the light is good for photos. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the tall buildings do not lean.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Porto, on Praça da Liberdade, with Avenida dos Aliados and its grand buildings about 150 m to the north of the stand-here point.
text.directions_text: Walk up the avenue to try the 'Porto' sign and the symmetrical view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to keep the statues and the buildings in one natural-looking frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the statues and the full height of the façades will not both fit. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Praça da Liberdade (quieter alternative, framing the avenue's buildings and the square's statues). Frame shots of the grand buildings lining the avenue, with the square's statues in the foreground. From here the grand buildings lining the avenue fill the background, and the square's statues give you a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a statue to one side of the frame and let the façades fill the rest, so the statue leads the eye up the avenue. Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with the vertical lines. If you want the 'Porto' sign or the symmetrical view of the City Hall, walk up the avenue and use those as a second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue or a building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Stay at 0.5x only when you need it, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: During the day, when the light is good for photos.

text.access_note: Praça da Liberdade and the avenue are open public spaces, but works or events may affect some angles, so check the situation on the day.
claims_not_in_sources: Praça da Liberdade and Avenida dos Aliados are in Porto city centre.
The avenue and the square are open public spaces with no entry charge.
Tilting a phone can make tall buildings appear to lean; gridlines help keep them upright.
Lowering exposure slightly helps keep detail in stonework when the sky is bright.
